newsitem.title: ITALY: Dini surprised by De Silguy EMU remarks - paper.
newsitem.headline: Dini surprised by De Silguy EMU remarks - paper.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was quoted on Saturday as saying European Economics Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy was wrong not to stress strict adherence to the Maastricht criteria on the single European currency.

In an interview in Friday's Daily Telegraph, De Silguy declined to rule out the possibility that countries with deficits above three percent of their gross domestic product would launch the single European currency.
The Maastricht treaty specifies a deficit to GDP ratio of three percent for entrants in economic and monetary union (EMU), the single currency.

"I can't answer for one criteria without all the elements - to be able to appreciate if we have a high degree of sustainable convergence," he said when asked if a country with a deficit of 3.5 percent of its GDP could join EMU.
He said countries wishing to join EMU should be close to the Maastricht reference values but added that there should be a "strict but not stupid" application of the treaty criteria.
Dini, a former central banker and prime minister, said he was surprised by De Silguy's comments.
"To pass to the third phase of monetary union, it is above all necessary to win the trust of the financial markets," Dini said in an interview with La Repubblica daily.

"It is true that the evaluation for the birth of the single currency will be a general and political one, but there is no doubt that a euro as strong as the mark requires the criteria to be respected by all participants," he said.
"And the markets must be given a sense of stability on this point, because this is the right way. But De Silguy seems to me to have gone down the wrong road," Dini said.

He added that he believed Italy had started to regain the trust of the markets thanks to its efforts to restore order to its chaotic state finances, which have led to low inflation and interest rate cuts.

"By now, the markets have come to believe that Italy will respect the Maastrict parametres. They can see that our inflation rate is lower than in Germany and France and they can also see how interet rates have dropped," he said.
